14. Working with lab values

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-14-labs.Rmd
book-14-labs.Rmd

What you will learn

Find a lab and its units; choose one value per person; convert units; form bins and flags; measure change; and pool summaries and a model across two connections.

You need: the packages, downloaded helpers and two loaded resources in Before you start, plus the recipe basics from chapter 6. Start a fresh R session in book-work. Run the sections in order: each uses objects defined immediately above it.

This chapter uses synthetic Synthea27Nj measurements, described in Getting started.

Concept selections refer to the searches and saved definitions in chapter 4, including the separate questionnaire catalogue. Additional body-measurement concepts are found on screen in the formula walkthrough.

Connect and find a lab

The shared connection file selects the driver, URL, project and resource names. Selecting numeric switches this lesson to Synthea without changing those settings.

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/connection.R")
source("tools/book/practice.R")
practice <- book_connect("numeric")
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
#> [1] "site"

Search the vocabulary first. A concept identifies what was measured; it does not identify a patient. Hemoglobin is the vocabulary’s spelling of haemoglobin.

hits <- ds.omop.concept.search("Hemoglobin", domain = "Measurement", conns = conns)
knitr::kable(head(hits$pooled[c("concept_name", "domain_id", "vocabulary_id")], 6))
concept_name domain_id vocabulary_id
Hemoglobin and Hematocrit panel - Blood Measurement LOINC
Hemoglobin A1c/Hemoglobin.total in Blood Measurement LOINC
Hemoglobin.gastrointestinal.lower [Presence] in Stool by Immunoassay –1st specimen Measurement LOINC
Hemoglobin [Presence] in Urine by Test strip Measurement LOINC
Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood Measurement LOINC

Select the blood mass-concentration concept deliberately. Other hemoglobin concepts can describe a different test. IDs in code select public vocabulary; shown tables use their names.

lab_id <- hits$pooled$concept_id[hits$pooled$concept_name == "Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood"]
chosen <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(lab_id, conns = conns)
knitr::kable(chosen$pooled[c("concept_name", "domain_id")])
concept_name domain_id
Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood Measurement

Now ask which units were recorded for this concept. This is a checked aggregate, not a download of measurement rows.

unit_counts <- ds.omop.value.counts("measurement", "unit_concept_id",
  concept_id = lab_id, scope = "pooled", conns = conns)
knitr::kable(unit_counts$pooled[c("concept_name", "n")])
concept_name n
gram per deciliter 105

The record count is disclosure-banded; it is not an exact patient count. The recorded unit is grams per deciliter (g/dL). The analyst sees the protected aggregate above.

Exercise. Look up the name of unit 8713. Does a vocabulary lookup prove that any patient has a result in that unit?

Solution

unit_names <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(8713L, conns = conns)
knitr::kable(unit_names$pooled["concept_name"])
concept_name
gram per deciliter

No. The lookup describes the unit; the preceding aggregate establishes recorded use.

Choose one value per person

An event selects records. Here it selects one lab and one recorded unit. A unit filter excludes other units; it does not convert them.

lab <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = lab_id, value = "value_as_number",
  unit = omop_unit(8713L))
class(lab)
#> [1] "omop_event" "list"

A reducer turns repeated readings into one number. First and last use the record dates (then source and record key for ties), whereas min and max use the size of the value. These reducers skip missing values by default.

first <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("first_value"))
last <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("last_value"))
class(first)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

The mean weights each available reading equally within a person. Min and max show that person’s observed range, not a clinical reference range.

average <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("mean"))
minimum <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("min"))
maximum <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("max"))
class(average)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

Omitting the window on these advanced reducers uses all recorded history. Assign a wide table, with one private row per person. Only its symbol returns.

values <- omop_recipe(variables = list(first = first, last = last,
  mean = average, minimum = minimum, maximum = maximum),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(values, out = c(people = "D_labs"), conns = conns))
#>   people 
#> "D_labs"

Ask for an approved summary of the first values. All patient-level numbers remain on the server; the table below contains summary statistics only.

first_summary <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_labs$first", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(first_summary))

First is earliest in time; minimum is smallest in value. They answer different questions.

Exercise 2. Would a person with no eligible lab have first = 0?

Solution 2

No. First, last, mean, min and max are missing (NA) when no eligible nonmissing values exist. Zero would claim a measured value. The person-grain table still includes that person; this particular dataset has hemoglobin for everyone.

Compare reducers and their groupings

Keep the raw number and its grouping together. Use the same teaching threshold for first and last; grouping hides the size of differences within each category. The repeated mean in each row below is the overall mean of that raw column, not a category-specific mean. Only released aggregates are combined locally.

grouped <- omop_recipe(variables = list(first = first, last = last,
  first_group = omop_number_bins(first, breaks = c(-Inf, 14.5, Inf),
    labels = c("below 14.5", "14.5 or above")),
  last_group = omop_number_bins(last, breaks = c(-Inf, 14.5, Inf),
    labels = c("below 14.5", "14.5 or above"))))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(grouped, out = c(output = "D_reducer_groups"), conns = conns))
#>             output 
#> "D_reducer_groups"
first_groups <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reducer_groups$first_group", datasources = conns)
first_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_reducer_groups$first", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
last_groups <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reducer_groups$last_group", datasources = conns)
last_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_reducer_groups$last", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(rbind(book_group_comparison(first_groups, first_mean, "first", "g/dL"),
                  book_group_comparison(last_groups, last_mean, "last", "g/dL")))
Category Count Number Unit Mean

Every person still contributes once; reducing their readings and then grouping the result answers a different question from grouping each measurement first.

Anchor a value and estimate a slope

An index date is the reference date for each study episode. For this teaching example, choose seven days after each person’s first lab. The offset makes it clear that “at index” can use a nearby measurement rather than an exact-date match.

index <- omop_index(lab, offset = 7L)
class(index)
#> [1] "omop_index" "list"

Tolerance c(-7, 0) includes the preceding seven days and index day, never a later reading. The shortcut selects the closest eligible nonmissing value.

indexed <- omop_study(index, outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
  at_index = omop_value_at_index("measurement", lab_id,
    tolerance = c(-7, 0), unit = 8713L)))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(indexed, out = c(baseline = "D_lab_index"), conns = conns))
#>      baseline 
#> "D_lab_index"

Read its summary. If no measurement falls inside the tolerance the value is missing, even when that person has measurements elsewhere in their history.

index_summary <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_lab_index$at_index", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(index_summary))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 11.810
site 10% 12.480
site 25% 12.975
site 50% 13.700
site 75% 15.425
site 90% 16.190
site 95% 16.855
site Mean 14.150

A slope fits a straight line to value against date within each person. It uses all eligible readings, unlike first-to-last subtraction. The unit here is g/dL per day. At least two distinct measurement dates are needed.

slopes <- omop_recipe(variables = list(per_day = omop_variable(event = lab,
  reducer = omop_reduce("slope"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(slopes, out = c(people = "D_lab_slopes"), conns = conns))
#>         people 
#> "D_lab_slopes"

Summarise the slopes, not the private fitted lines.

slope_summary <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_lab_slopes$per_day", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(slope_summary))

site 95% 0.0011030

Declare a common unit

To pool measurements, first align their meaning and units. Look up the target unit grams per liter (g/L).

target_unit <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(8636L, conns = conns)
knitr::kable(target_unit$pooled["concept_name"])
concept_name
gram per liter

Declare the conversion: g/dL multiplied by ten becomes g/L. Rows already in g/L retain their value. Other units become missing by default; the server never guesses a conversion. unknown = "exclude" would drop those rows instead.

lab_gl <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = lab_id,
  unit = omop_unit(8636L, convert = list("8713" = c(factor = 10, offset = 0))))
class(lab_gl)
#> [1] "omop_event" "list"

The conversion precedes predicates and reducers, and also transforms recorded reference bounds. This source only has g/dL for this lab; we are converting its actual values, not inventing a mixed-unit source.

converted <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean_gl = omop_variable(event = lab_gl,
  reducer = omop_reduce("mean"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(converted, out = c(people = "D_lab_gl"), conns = conns))
#>     people 
#> "D_lab_gl"

Exercise. Summarise the converted means. How should they compare with the g/dL summary above?

Solution

conversion_summary <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_lab_gl$mean_gl", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(conversion_summary))

Every displayed quantile and the mean is ten times its earlier value. Use the same target unit and declared conversion map at every site before pooling.

Round and bin without losing the raw number

Keep a raw mean, a rounded mean and a band from the same declaration. Native bins are ordered factors on the server, with every declared level retained. The mean is reduced before rounding and binning; these are public teaching cutoffs, not clinical reference limits.

band_levels <- c("below 14", "14 to below 15", "15 or above")
flags <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean = average,
  rounded = omop_number(average, omop_number_spec(rounding = omop_number_round("decimals", 1))),
  band = omop_number_bins(average, breaks = c(-Inf, 14, 15, Inf), labels = band_levels),
  high = omop_number_flag(average, "ge", 15),
  low = omop_number_flag(average, "lt", 14)))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(flags, out = c(output = "D_lab_flags"), conns = conns))
#>        output 
#> "D_lab_flags"
bin_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_lab_flags$band", useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(bin_counts))
Category Count
below 14 9
14 to below 15 9
15 or above 10
NA 0

Unlike the old mutate-plus-cut workaround, the factor is ordered before release. That affects model contrasts: choose the raw number or explicit contrasts when a linear ordinal effect is not the model you intend.

Use low, normal and high explicitly

For an aggregate such as a mean, supply public thresholds. “Normal” here only means the middle interval of this teaching rule. It is not a diagnosis.

category_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(control =
  omop_number_category(average, range = "thresholds", thresholds = c(14, 15))))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(category_recipe, out = c(output = "D_control"), conns = conns))
#>      output 
#> "D_control"
knitr::kable(book_counts(dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_control$control", datasources = conns)))
Category Count
low 9
normal 9
high 10
NA 0

Reference mode instead uses the bounds paired with the selected observation. Synthea27Nj records no bounds for haemoglobin, so this example deliberately shows the source-validation refusal for missing reference bounds. The missing bounds cannot establish normality. Do not invent bounds or weaken the release check to obtain categories. The declared-threshold example above is the runnable alternative when those cutoffs are part of the protocol.

The refusal can also emit the DSLite cleanup warning shown below: an internal execution handle has already been removed. It is a cleanup diagnostic, not a released patient count or a successful assignment. Its temporary handle name changes between sessions. Both diagnostics remain visible in this lesson.

reference_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(control = omop_number_category(last, range = "reference")))
reference_message <- tryCatch({
  recipe_execute(reference_recipe, out = c(output = "D_reference"), conns = conns)
  "Reference output assigned"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> Warning in rm(list = c(name), envir = private$.session(sid)): object 'dsOexec.tHBajA'
#> not found
cat(reference_message, "\n")
#> Plan publication refused: site:output [validation_error] (number_source_invalid). Execution-owned artifacts were revoked and removed.

Category Count
0 18

The flag is a numeric 0/1 value with missing inputs preserved. Its threshold belongs to the coordinate being classified, here g/dL after reduction.

Compose conversion, rounding and classification

A pipeline fixes the order. Convert g/dL to g/L, round to one decimal, then classify using cutoffs in g/L. Rounding can move a value across a cutoff; classifying before rounding answers a different question.

presentation <- omop_number_pipeline(
  omop_number_unit("unit:8713", "unit:8636", factor = 10),
  omop_number_round("decimals", 1),
  omop_number_spec(representation = "bins", breaks = c(0, 140, 150, 1000),
    labels = c("below 140", "140 to below 150", "150 or above")))
pipeline_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(band = omop_number(average, presentation)))
explanation <- recipe_explain(pipeline_recipe, detail = "semantics")
cat(grep("numeric|unit:|round|pipeline|levels", explanation$text, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#> Federation: permitted ID union, including declared unused levels; newest comparable vocabulary version, then bytewise name tie. Unresolved versions never establish recency.
#> Precedence: variable/wrapper > recipe > design; pipelines are atomic. Canonical inputs bypass transforms/rounds/categories and outer recipe defaults.
#> Public bins/categories retain full ordered levels and polynomial contrasts; quantitative trends require a numeric sibling. Reference categories are relative to each selected observation's paired local ranges.
#> Required numeric capabilities: number.presentation
#> Numeric variable 'band': {"broadcast":false,"column_names":{},"labels":{},"number_spec":{"pipeline":[{"factor":10,"from":"unit:8713","kind":"fixed_unit","offset":0,"to":"unit:8636"},{"digits":1,"kind":"round","method":"decimals"},{"breaks":[0,140,150,1000],"closed":"left","kind":"bins","labels":["below 140","140 to below 150","150 or above"]}]},"reducer":{"agg":null,"coverage":"recorded","distinct":null,"fills":"start_in_window","fn":"mean","missing":"skip","n":1,"observed_only":false,"p":null,"predicate":null,"reference":null,"reference_date":null,"side":"either","unit":"day","value":"value","which":null,"window":null},"source":{"event":"lab_3000963"}}; source/reducer grain retained; broadcast=FALSE; date/class-2 lineage never declassified.
#>   specification origin: variable/wrapper; explicit declaration: {"pipeline":[{"factor":10,"from":"unit:8713","kind":"fixed_unit","offset":0,"to":"unit:8636"},{"digits":1,"kind":"round","method":"decimals"},{"breaks":[0,140,150,1000],"kind":"bins","labels":["below 140","140 to below 150","150 or above"]}]}
#>   canonical source coordinate: unit:8713
#>   stage 1 fixed_unit: numeric -> numeric; coordinate unit:8636; private scalar presentation before sealing
#>   stage 2 round: numeric -> numeric; coordinate unit:8636; private scalar presentation before sealing
#>   stage 3 bins: numeric -> ordered factor (contr.poly); coordinate unit:8636; complete public levels: below 140 | 140 to below 150 | 150 or above; private scalar presentation before sealing

Read the declared coordinate, stage order and complete public level set. No private distribution is needed to explain a public presentation rule.

book_symbols(recipe_execute(pipeline_recipe, out = c(output = "D_pipeline"), conns = conns))
#>       output 
#> "D_pipeline"
knitr::kable(book_counts(dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_pipeline$band", datasources = conns)))
Category Count
below 140 9
140 to below 150 9
150 or above 10
NA 0

Change over time and first observed attainment

Difference is last minus first. Percent change divides that difference by first; ratio divides last by first. A zero baseline cannot support either division. Slope uses actual elapsed time. Time to threshold is first observed attainment, without interpolation; missing attainment is not evidence of permanent failure.

changes <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  change = omop_number_change(lab, "difference"),
  percent = omop_number_change(lab, "percent_change"),
  ratio = omop_number_change(lab, "ratio"),
  per_day = omop_number_change(lab, "slope", time_unit = "days"),
  target_days = omop_number_change(lab, "time_to_threshold", threshold = 14,
    op = "ge", reference = "first", time_unit = "days")))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(changes, out = c(output = "D_lab_change"), conns = conns))
#>         output 
#> "D_lab_change"
change_summary <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_lab_change$change", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(change_summary))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% -2.940
site 10% -2.580
site 25% -1.400
site 50% 1.600
site 75% 2.400
site 90% 3.200
site 95% 3.760
site Mean 1.016

A single observed value produces missing native change: two eligible readings are required. Subtracting separately reduced first and last would instead give zero for that person, which would falsely suggest an observed change. Measurement frequency affects observed attainment times.

site 95% 4166.750
site Mean 1274.808

Day zero means the first eligible reading already met the threshold. A person who never attains it has a missing time; use an explicit censored survival design for a time-to-event analysis rather than dropping those people.

Several columns from one output value

Output-column declarations copy a numeric value privately with its row identity and privacy lineage. They do not join unrelated measurement rows.

column_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean = average),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person", columns = c("mean", "mean_rounded"),
    number_columns = list(mean_rounded = omop_number_column("mean",
      number_spec = omop_number_spec(rounding = omop_number_round("decimals", 1))))))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(column_recipe, out = c(people = "D_number_columns"), conns = conns))
#>             people 
#> "D_number_columns"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_number_columns", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"    "mean"         "mean_rounded"

The stable input key is mean, before presentation renames. Canonical numeric inputs bypass display settings; explicitly presented inputs must still be numeric. An ordered bin cannot be fed back into arithmetic as if it were the original value.

Exercise. Verify that the copied rounded column has the same summary as the earlier rounded column.

Solution: column copy

knitr::kable(book_summary(dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_number_columns$mean_rounded", datasources = conns)))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 12.90500
site 10% 13.17000
site 25% 13.77500
site 50% 14.30000
site 75% 15.32500
site 90% 15.69000
site 95% 15.96500
site Mean 14.45714

Compare this aggregate with the native-types solution above. The row grain and rounding declaration are the same.

Pool across two connections

This section is a local DSLite exercise, even if the earlier sections used Opal. The helper creates temporary, disjoint copies of the public Synthea data: 14 people in north, 14 in south. It preserves their measurements and units, then logs into two actual DSLite servers. It never partitions a live Opal dataset. A real multisite analysis instead supplies its authorised connections and must establish that populations do not overlap.

pair <- book_numeric_pair()
two_conns <- pair$conns
names(two_conns)
#> [1] "north" "south"

Run the identical native recipe at both sites. A lab column has the same meaning, unit, missing-value rule and person-level grain at each site.

book_symbols(recipe_execute(values, out = c(people = "D_pool_labs"), conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#>        people 
#> "D_pool_labs"

ds.mean combines nonmissing observations across sites. Here each observation is one person’s mean lab value, so each person receives equal weight.

pooled_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_pool_labs$mean", type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)
pooled_mean
#> $Global.Mean
#>                 EstimatedMean Nmissing Nvalid Ntotal
#> studiesCombined      14.46679        0     28     28
#> 
#> $Nstudies
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $ValidityMessage
#>       ValidityMessage 
#> north "VALID ANALYSIS"
#> south "VALID ANALYSIS"

ds.quantileMean averages site quantiles with site-size weights. It is an estimate of the combined distribution, not the exact quantiles of concatenated patient values. Its mean agrees with the pooled mean here because all 28 person-level means are present. Missing data require care with denominators.

pooled_quantiles <- dsBaseClient::ds.quantileMean("D_pool_labs$mean",
  type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Statistic = names(pooled_quantiles), Value = as.numeric(pooled_quantiles)))
Statistic Value
5% 13.02050
10% 13.29000
25% 13.85104
50% 14.28917
75% 15.30625
90% 15.72500
95% 15.91000
Mean 14.46679

A Gaussian generalised linear model (GLM) relates a numeric outcome to a covariate. Fit last hemoglobin as the outcome and first hemoglobin as the covariate, both in g/dL. The servers keep the person-level data; the analyst sees model coefficients and diagnostics.

With dsBase 6.3.5, the call emits the warnings shown below: its local setup fits use maxit = 1. The distributed algorithm then iterates across sites; this example finishes in three iterations. The book’s independent checks compare its final coefficients, standard errors and deviance with a central Gaussian fit on the public synthetic source. Do not ignore an unexplained warning in a new study.

pooled_model <- dsBaseClient::ds.glm(formula = "last ~ first", data = "D_pool_labs",
  family = "gaussian", datasources = two_conns)
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
knitr::kable(pooled_model$coefficients)
Estimate Std. Error z-value p-value low0.95CI high0.95CI
(Intercept) 15.6082485 2.0915966 7.4623606 0.000000 11.508794 19.7077026
first -0.0511516 0.1479754 -0.3456763 0.729586 -0.341178 0.2388749

The first coefficient is the fitted difference in last hemoglobin for a one-g/dL difference in first hemoglobin. The intercept is the prediction at first = 0, far outside these data. This small synthetic example teaches mechanics; it is not a causal result or a validated prediction model.

Exercise 1. Pool the first-value means. Would opening two connections to the same 28 people be a valid way to increase the sample size?

Solution 1

pooled_first <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_pool_labs$first", type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)
pooled_first
#> $Global.Mean
#>                 EstimatedMean Nmissing Nvalid Ntotal
#> studiesCombined      13.98571        0     28     28
#> 
#> $Nstudies
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $ValidityMessage
#>       ValidityMessage 
#> north "VALID ANALYSIS"
#> south "VALID ANALYSIS"

No. Duplicate people would be counted twice, and model uncertainty would be misleading. These temporary sites instead have disjoint people.

Exercise 2. Is the mean of the two site medians necessarily the median you would get from all 28 people together?

Solution 2

No. These sites are equally sized, so ds.quantileMean averages their medians equally. In general that differs from the median of the combined observations; with unequal site sizes the function uses unequal weights.

Recap

Start with a lab meaning and its recorded units. Choose the person-level reducer and time window before releasing summaries. Declare conversions, distinguish teaching cutoffs from recorded reference bounds, and distinguish change from slope. Pool only compatible variables from nonoverlapping sites, and interpret ds.quantileMean according to its weighted-site definition.
